docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
An example of a client/server [Flutter] / [NestJS]

created by Anthropic’s AI Claude, reviewed by Serge Tahé - September 2026

This document is a translation of the original French version, generated using an automated tool. Some expressions or technical terms may not fully reflect the original meaning.

This course offers a mobile version of RdvMedecins, a doctor’s appointment-booking application: a Flutter client, written in Dart, that relies on a NestJS server exposing a JSON API protected by JWT authentication (ADMIN / USER roles).

It begins with setting up the working environment (Visual Studio Code, Flutter SDK, Android Studio, Android phone and emulator, flutter doctor), then installing the NestJS server, used here as a black box: you run it and test it, without studying its code.

It then introduces Flutter (widgets, StatelessWidget and StatefulWidget, state management with provider), studies the application’s client file by file, and ports the same source code to three families of targets: mobile (Android, iOS), desktop (Windows, macOS, Linux) and web, with the pitfalls specific to mobile.

The course is aimed at readers who already know a web framework (Angular, React or Vue.js) and discover Flutter by comparison: each Flutter concept is related to its equivalent in these frameworks. The basics of the Dart language are presented in the course Introduction to the Dart Language Through Examples.

The same application is built with web clients in the Angular / NestJS, React / NestJS and Vue.js / NestJS courses. To learn Flutter from small examples, see the course Step-by-Step Introduction to the Flutter Mobile Framework.

All courses by Serge Tahé

2.1. Install the tools
docs.text:
1. Node.js: Download and install version 22 (or later) from nodejs.org. Verify the installation in a terminal: 
    node --version
npm --version
  1. Visual Studio Code (VSCode): available for free download at code.visualstudio.com. Install the “TypeScript and JavaScript Language Features” extension (usually already included).
  1. [MySQL] 8: Install, for example, via XAMPP, Laragon (on Windows), or directly via [MySQL] Community Server. A graphical administration tool (phpMyAdmin, [MySQL] Workbench, DBeaver, HeidiSQL…) simplifies the process. Subsequently, the Laragon tool is used.
  2. Postman: available for free download at postman.com.

docs.title: 2.1.2. Android Studio and Android Command-Line Tools
docs.text:
The mobile target for this course is a [Android] phone. To compile the app and install it on this phone, [Flutter] requires SDK and [Android], which are installed along with [Android Studio], Google’s development environment. [Android Studio] is not used for writing code—the editor remains [VSCode]—it is used here only to install and update SDK and [Android].

  1. [Android Studio]: Download it for free from [https://developer.android.com/studio] and then install it. When you launch it for the first time, the wizard will offer a standard installation: accept it, and it will download SDK and [Android].

  1. Open [SDK Manager] from [Android Studio] (the [Tools / SDK Manager] menu when a project is open, or [More Actions / SDK Manager] from the home screen): This is the tool that installs and updates the components of SDK and [Android].
  2. [SDK Platforms] tab: Verify that a recent [Android] platform is installed (the [Flutter] documentation specifies version 36 at the time of writing).

  1. [SDK Tools] tab: Check [Android SDK Command-line Tools (latest)], [Android SDK Build-Tools], and [Android SDK Platform-Tools] (as well as [Android Emulator] if you want to test on an emulator), then click [Apply]. The documentation for [Flutter] also recommends [CMake] and [NDK (Side by side)]. It is the [Android SDK Command-line Tools] packages that are missing when [flutter doctor] displays “cmdline-tools component is missing.”
  2. Accept the licenses for SDK and [Android] by typing the following command in a terminal within the Flutter project, then answering “[y]” to each question until you see the message “All SDK package licenses accepted.”: 
    flutter doctor –android-licenses

[Remarque]: With version 23.0 of [Android SDK Command-line Tools], the command above may terminate immediately, without prompting for anything, displaying “The --licenses option is no longer needed.” This is a known issue in [Flutter] (issues 191558 and 191487 on github.com/flutter/flutter). Workaround: In [SDK Manager], [SDK Tools] tab, check [Show Package Details], replace version 23.0 of [Android SDK Command-line Tools] with version 22.0, click on [Apply], and then rerun the command.

docs.title: 2.1.3. Create on an Android emulator
docs.text:
If you don’t have a phone, you can test the app on a [Android] emulator: a virtual phone that runs in a window on your computer. [Android Studio] installs the [Android Emulator] program (if it was checked in the [SDK Manager], see above) but does not provide a ready-to-use virtual device: you must create one.

  1. [Prérequis]: Virtualization must be enabled in the computer’s [BIOS], and under [Windows], the [Plateforme de l'hyperviseur Windows] feature must be checked ([Panneau de configuration / Programmes / Activer ou désactiver des fonctionnalités Windows]), which requires a restart. Otherwise, the emulator will not start or will remain very slow.
  2. Open [Device Manager] from [Android Studio]: [More Actions / Virtual Device Manager] from the home screen, or [Tools / Device Manager] when a project is open (depending on the version: [View / Tool Windows / Device Manager]).

  1. Click on [Create Device], select a template (for example, [Pixel 8]), then [Next]. Select a recent [Android] system image for the [x86_64] processor and download it using the [Download] link located next to it, then [Next] and [Finish].

  1. Start the emulator using the [Play] button on the [Device Manager], or from a terminal (the first command lists the emulators and their IDs): 
    flutter emulators
flutter emulators --launch <id>

  1. Wait until the [Android] welcome screen appears in the emulator window: the first startup may take several minutes. Then verify that [Flutter] recognizes the emulator, which should appear in the list (for example, [emulator-5554], platform [android-x64]): 
flutter devices


PS C:\Data\st-2026\dev\flutter-nestjs-sept-2026\rdvmedecins_flutter_client> flutter devices
Found 4 connected devices:
  sdk gphone16k x86 64 (mobile) • emulator-5554 • android-x64    • Android 17 (API 37) (emulator)
  Windows (desktop)             • windows       • windows-x64    • Microsoft Windows [version
  10.0.26200.9457]
  Chrome (web)                  • chrome        • web-javascript • Google Chrome 153.0.8010.48
  Edge (web)                    • edge          • web-javascript • Microsoft Edge 153.0.4234.48

[Remarque]: if [flutter devices] does not display the emulator but instead shows the message “Device emulator-5554 is offline,” the emulator has not finished starting up, or [adb] (the tool that connects the computer to the device, installed along with [Android SDK Platform-Tools]) is in an inconsistent state. Try the following in order: (1) wait for the welcome screen to appear, then rerun the command; (2) restart [adb] using the following three commands (in [Windows], within [PowerShell]), with the last one displaying “device” rather than “offline”; (3) In the [Device Manager], under the device’s [⋮] menu, select [Cold Boot Now], or even [Wipe Data] as a last resort.

& "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Android\Sdk\platform-tools\adb.exe" kill-server
& "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Android\Sdk\platform-tools\adb.exe" start-server
& "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Android\Sdk\platform-tools\adb.exe" devices

If the problem persists, use [where.exe adb] to verify that no other [adb], of a different version, is present in the [PATH]: Two versions of [adb] competing for the connection cause this issue.

Once the emulator is recognized, the application launches on it with the following command. Note: In the emulator, [localhost] refers to the emulator itself and not the computer; the “URL on the server” field must contain [http://10.0.2.2:8080] (see Chapter 5).

flutter run -d emulator-5554

docs.title: 2.1.4. Preparing the Android phone
docs.text:
To run the app on a real [Android] phone, the phone must be set to allow control from the computer:

  1. Enable developer options: open [Paramètres / À propos du téléphone], then tap [Numéro de build] several times (usually 7) until the phone indicates that you are a developer. The exact labels vary by manufacturer.
  2. Enable [Débogage USB] in the [Options pour les développeurs] menu (added in the previous step).
  3. Connect the phone to the computer using a USB cable that transfers data (not just charges the phone), and accept the USB debugging permission request on the phone. On Windows, if the phone is not recognized, install the manufacturer’s driver USB (“OEM USB drivers,” see [https://developer.android.com/studio/run/oem-usb]).
  4. Verify that [Flutter] detects the phone: it should appear in the list displayed by the following command, along with the [android] platform: 
    flutter devices

The phone will access the [NestJS] server via the computer’s IP address on the local network (and not via [localhost]): this configuration is described in Chapter 5.

docs.title: 3. Chapter 2 - Installing the [NestJS] server
docs.text:
The [Flutter] client described in this document requires a server to query: the [NestJS] server for the [RdvMedecins] application, included with this document in the [rdvmedecins-nestjs-server] folder. Since this document focuses on [Flutter], that server is treated as a “black box”: this chapter explains how to install it, configure it, create its [MySQL] database, launch it, and test it, but does not examine its code. Readers who wish to learn [NestJS] can refer to the document *Introduction to the TypeScript Language and the NestJS Framework* (2026).

This chapter is essentially a reprint of the chapter “Installing a NestJS Server” from the document *Introduction to the Dart Language Through Examples* (2026), adapted for a different server: the tax calculation server in that document is replaced here by the [RdvMedecins] server, and its [dbimpots-2019] database by the [dbrdvmedecins] database.

docs.title: 3.1. Installing Laragon
docs.text:
To create the [MySQL] database used by the [NestJS] server, we will use the Laragon tool. As of September 2026, Laragon is available at URL and [Download Laragon – Fast & Modern Dev Environment ]. Laragon includes tools that allow you to install a PHP server and the SGBD and [MySQL] servers:

  • in [1], an Apache web server;
  • into [2], the SGBD and [MySQL];
  • to [3], a messaging tool that we will not be using;
  • [4] starts all services (Apache, [MySQL], MailPit);
  • [5] displays the web page for URL and [http://localhost]. By default, this URL refers to the <laragon-install>\www folder, where <laragon-install> is the Laragon installation folder;
  • in [6], launches the HeidiSQL tool, which allows you to manage MySQL databases. We will use this tool to create the database used by the [RdvMedecins] server;
  • In [7], open a terminal where all the binaries needed for Laragon are located in PATH;
  • In [8], open Windows File Explorer to the folder associated with URL and [http://localhost];

The Laragon installation folder contains the following items:

  • In [1], the [bin] folder contains numerous applications:
  • In [1], the Apache web server;
  • in [2], a command-line terminal;
  • in [3], a [git] client for versioning different versions of a project;
  • in [4], a database manager;
  • in [5], a mail manager;
  • in [6], the SGBD and [MySQL];
  • [7], another web server;
  • in [8], [node.js] to run JavaScript scripts;
  • [9], a text editor;
  • [10], the PHP interpreter;
  • [11], the [Python] interpreter;
  • [12], a cache server;

Laragon comes with a comprehensive development environment. In this course, we will use only SGBD, [MySQL], [6], and the [heidisql] tool to manage it graphically;

docs.title: 3.2. Installation and Configuration of the [NestJS] Server
docs.text:
The [rdvmedecins-nestjs-server] folder has the following directory structure:

rdvmedecins-nestjs-server/
├── package.json                  # npm dependencies and scripts
├── tsconfig.json                 # QZXW2HTML compiler configuration CVHlwZVNjcmlwdAZQX
├── nest-cli.json                 # CLI configuration NestJS
├── .env.example                  # .env configuration file template
├── database/
│   └── dbrdvmedecins.sql         # database creation script
└── src/
    ├── main.ts                   # server entry point
    ├── app.module.ts             # root module
    ├── config/                   # database connection
    ├── entities/                 # entities TypeORM (one class per table)
    ├── domain/                   # business objects
    ├── repositories/             # data access (DAO layer)
    ├── metier/                   # business layer
    ├── web/                      # JSON controller and response templates
    └── auth/                     # JWT authentication and roles

Each subfolder of [src/] contains its own [README.md] file, which summarizes the purpose of the files it contains. The source code for these files is not covered in this document.

In the [rdvmedecins-nestjs-server] folder, type the following commands in a terminal:

npm install
cp .env.example .env

The [.env] file sets environment variables:

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Sample configuration file.
# Copy this file to [.env], then adjust the values for your machine.
# The [.env] file must never be shared or committed (passwords).
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------

# listening port for the NestJS server (the original Spring server listened on port 8080)
PORT=8080

# Database connection parameters: MySQL, [dbrdvmedecins]
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=3306
DB_USERNAME=root
DB_PASSWORD=
DB_DATABASE=dbrdvmedecins

# for development only: TypeORM can automatically create/update
# tables from entities. We disable this here because we provide our
# own script SQL [database/dbrdvmedecins.sql], just as the original Spring project did.
DB_SYNCHRONIZE=false

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
# authentication (see src/auth/)
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
# secret key used to sign/verify tokens JWT - to be changed
# must be changed in production (a long random string, never committed).
JWT_SECRET=change-moi-en-une-longue-chaine-aleatoire
# validity period of a token JWT (see the [ms] library documentation:
# "60", "2h", "7d"...)
JWT_EXPIRES_IN=2h

Adapt the newly created [.env] file to your [MySQL] installation (username, password, port). Since authentication was added, this file also contains a key named JWT_SECRET: the example value is suitable for following along with this document, but must be replaced with a random string unique to you before any actual use.

docs.title: 3.3. Creating the Database
docs.text: The [dbrdvmedecins] database mirrors the structure of the original document (2014, Spring 4 / [MySQL] 5): same tables—[medecins], [clients], [creneaux], [rv]—same foreign keys, same uniqueness constraint. The only new addition, introduced by the “authentication” step of this port: the table [users]. The relationships between these tables are as follows: a doctor ([medecins]) has several time slots ([creneaux], foreign key [id_medecin]); an appointment ([rv]) links a day, a time slot (and thus a doctor), and a client ([clients]); the table [users] is independent of the other four: it is used solely for authentication.

docs.title: 3.3.1. [database/dbrdvmedecins.sql]
docs.text:
-- =========================================================================
  -- Database [dbrdvmedecins] - MySQL 8
  --
  -- This script uses EXACTEMENT the relational schema of the original document
  -- (2014, Spring 4 / Spring Data / MySQL 5): same tables, same columns,
  -- same foreign keys, same uniqueness constraint. Only the database engine
  -- is renamed (MySQL 5 -> MySQL 8), not the structure.
  --
  -- The original document used TROIS tables (users, roles,
 -- users_roles) to allow a user to have PLUSIEURS roles.
 -- Since this application recognizes only two mutually
 -- (ADMIN, USER), we simplify here to a single column [role]
 -- in the table [users] rather than reconstructing the original many-to-
 -- multiple relationship—a deliberate simplification for educational purposes, documented
 -- in the "Authentication" chapter of the course.
 -- =========================================================================

 -- We start with an empty database each time the script runs (useful during development)
 DROP TABLE IF EXISTS rv;
 DROP TABLE IF EXISTS creneaux;
 DROP TABLE IF EXISTS clients;
 DROP TABLE IF EXISTS medecins;
 DROP TABLE IF EXISTS users;

 CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS dbrdvmedecins CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_ci;
 USE dbrdvmedecins;

 CREATE TABLE medecins (
   id      INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
   version INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
   titre   VARCHAR(5)  NOT NULL,
   nom     VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
   prenom  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL
 );

 CREATE TABLE clients (
   id      INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
   version INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
   titre   VARCHAR(5)  NOT NULL,
   nom     VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
   prenom  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL
 );

 CREATE TABLE creneaux (
   id         INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
   version    INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
   id_medecin INT NOT NULL,
   hdebut     INT NOT NULL,
   mdebut     INT NOT NULL,
   hfin       INT NOT NULL,
   mfin       INT NOT NULL,
   CONSTRAINT fk_creneaux_medecin FOREIGN KEY (id_medecin) REFERENCES medecins(id)
 );

 CREATE TABLE rv (
   id         INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
   version    INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
   jour       DATE NOT NULL,
   id_creneau INT NOT NULL,
   id_client  INT NOT NULL,
   CONSTRAINT fk_rv_creneau FOREIGN KEY (id_creneau) REFERENCES creneaux(id),
   CONSTRAINT fk_rv_client  FOREIGN KEY (id_client)  REFERENCES clients(id),
   CONSTRAINT unq1_rv UNIQUE (jour, id_creneau)
 );

 CREATE TABLE users (
   id       INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
   version  INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
   login    VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
   password VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
   nom      VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
   role     VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL
 );

 INSERT INTO medecins (titre, nom, prenom) VALUES
   ('Mme', 'PELISSIER', 'Marie'), ('Mr', 'TATOU', 'Paul'), ('Melle','DUPONT', 'Sophie');

 INSERT INTO clients (titre, nom, prenom) VALUES
   ('Mr', 'MARTIN', 'Jean'), ('Mme', 'DURAND', 'Alice'),
   ('Melle','BISTROU', 'Brigitte'), ('Mr', 'GERMAN', 'Luc');

 INSERT INTO creneaux (id_medecin, hdebut, mdebut, hfin, mfin) VALUES
   (1, 8, 0, 8, 20), (1, 8, 20, 8, 40), /* ... */ (1, 11, 40, 12, 0);

 INSERT INTO creneaux (id_medecin, hdebut, mdebut, hfin, mfin) VALUES
   (2, 14, 0, 14, 20), (2, 14, 20, 14, 40), /* ... */ (2, 17, 40, 18, 0);

 INSERT INTO rv (jour, id_creneau, id_client) VALUES (CURDATE(), 2, 3);

 INSERT INTO users (login, password, nom, role) VALUES
   ('admin', '$2b$10$YSNBJXXHX9mp13nPZb6YGu8M1jR6uvPwO1s2X73z0QAqBR7TOQjoq', 'Administrateur', 'ADMIN'),
   ('user',  '$2b$10$6Cvoion7AgJkpYHw5N0jMuWPf8T90J28En56kWBL9PT0bXt7lwW7.', 'Utilisateur',    'USER');

Let’s comment on this code:

  • Lines 20–24: [DROP TABLE IF EXISTS …] — the script starts with an empty database on each execution, in the reverse order of dependencies (starting with `rv`, which references `[creneaux]` and `clients`, all the way down to `users`, which is not referenced by anyone): [MySQL] would refuse to delete a table still referenced by a foreign key;
  • line 48: [id_medecin INT NOT NULL], then line 53: [CONSTRAINT fk_creneaux_medecin FOREIGN KEY …] — a time slot always belongs to a doctor;
  • line 64: [CONSTRAINT unq1_rv UNIQUE (jour, id_creneau)] — the application’s central business rule: the same time slot on the same day can be booked only once. It is this constraint, and this constraint alone, that prevents a duplicate appointment—neither the validator nor the business layer explicitly rechecks it;
  • lines 67–74: [CREATE TABLE users (…)] — the table added by this step. `login` is UNIQUE (two users cannot share the same login ID); `password` stores a password hashed using bcrypt (never in plaintext); role is either 'ADMIN' or 'USER'—a simple text column, whereas the original document used three tables (users, roles, users_roles) to allow multiple roles per user. Since this application requires only two mutually exclusive roles, the original many-to-many relationship would have been more than necessary;
  • lines 91–93: [INSERT INTO users …] — two demo accounts, admin/admin (role ADMIN) and user/user (role USER), with their passwords already hashed using bcrypt (10 rounds of salting)—never in plaintext, including in this demo script.

docs.title: 3.3.2. Running the script with HeidiSQL
docs.text:
To create the [MySQL] database required by the [NestJS] server, we proceed as follows:

  • In [1], all services must be started;
  • in [2], the [Database] option allows you to manage the database;

The [Database] option launches a utility called HeidiSQL:

  • In [1], you can select various SGBD options. The default value provided is SGBD MySQL. This is acceptable;
  • in [2], you log in to HeidiSQL;

Business responses are wrapped in a [{ status, data }] object, where [status] is set to 0 upon success.

docs.title: 4.1. Sources
docs.text: Official documentation: https://docs.flutter.dev—in particular the pages “What is Flutter?”, “Introduction to widgets,” and “State management.” [Dart] language: https://dart.dev/language

docs.title: 4.2. What Flutter Is Not EST PAS
docs.text:
This is the most important starting point for this chapter, as it differs significantly from the three previous versions of this course. [Angular], [React], and [Vue.js] all produce [JavaScript]/[TypeScript] COMPILÉ, which is executed by the [JavaScript] engine already present in a browser—this engine handles all the display work, via [DOM] and [CSS]. A tool like [Cordova]/[Capacitor] (not used in this course) does allow you to package such a web client into a mobile shell, but the client then continues to run in an embedded browser (a [WebView])—never natively.

[Flutter] has nothing to do with any of this. The [Dart] code in this document is compiled, for both mobile and desktop, into NATIF machine code (compilation [AOT], [Ahead-Of-Time] —the same compilation family as a C++ or Rust program), which is directly executable by the target operating system; it does not require an interpreter such as SANS, [JavaScript], or [WebView] of any kind. [Flutter] includes its own graphics rendering engine ([Impeller], which replaced [Skia] as the default engine on mobile devices): the application draws each of its pixels itself, frame by frame, rather than delegating the display to the operating system’s native widgets (unlike [React Native], which is not used in this course and which instead drives the actual interface components of [Android]/[iOS]). It is this architectural choice that allows [Flutter] to render an identical interface across the three environments targeted by this document - there are no native operating system components whose appearance might vary from one platform to another.

On the [web] target, however, there is obviously no compilation to native machine code: [flutter build web] compiles the [Dart] code to [JavaScript] (or to [WebAssembly], a more recent target), which is executed by the browser—but this generated [JavaScript] does not manipulate PAS, [DOM], or [HTML] the way [Vue.js] does: it, too, renders directly onto a single element (or via automatically generated elements, depending on the chosen rendering mode), thereby reproducing the same appearance [Flutter] as on mobile and desktop rather than relying on [HTML] elements styled in [CSS].

docs.title: 4.3. The Flutter development model: everything is a widget
docs.text: [Angular], [React], and [Vue.js]—all three distinguish the LOGIQUE of a component ([TypeScript]) from its PRÉSENTATION (a [HTML] template, which may be separate or integrated depending on the framework—see Chapter 4 of the [Vue.js] document for this course, “Components: [.vue] files and [Composition API]”). [Flutter] completely eliminates this distinction: TOUT, within a [Flutter] interface, is a [Widget]—a button, text, margin, alignment, and background color are each a widget, and a complete interface is nothing more than a ARBRE of widgets nested within one another, described by ordinary [Dart] code (the [build(BuildContext context)] method) rather than by a separate template language—in this respect, [Flutter] takes the choice already made by [React] ([JSX], from [JavaScript], which describes the interface) even further: whereas [JSX] remains a markup language—from MÊLÉ to [JavaScript]— [build(...)] simply returns a EXPRESSION [Dart]—nested constructor calls ([Scaffold(appBar: ..., body: Column(children: [...]))])—without any additional syntax to learn.

docs.title: 4.4. StatelessWidget and StatefulWidget: whereas Vue.js requires no distinction
docs.text: [Vue.js] (like [React] and [Angular] before it in this course) makes no structural distinction between a component that has a mutable state and one that does not: [ref(...)] may or may not be called within any [<script setup>], without changing anything in the component’s declaration itself. [Flutter] and IMPOSE make this distinction right from the class declaration: a [StatelessWidget] (nothing ever changes after its construction—see [AgendaView] and [LoginPage] in Chapter 4) redefines its method [build(...)] UNIQUEMENT when its parameters change; a [StatefulWidget] is duplicated as a separate [State<T>] class (see [_LoginFormState], [_AppRootState]..., Chapter 4), which holds the mutable state and the method [setState(() { ... })] —the call to EXPLICITE that triggers a new rendering, whereas [reactive(...)] on the [Vue.js] side automatically detects every property write. This separation into two classes (Widget/State) is a direct result of a deliberate design choice in [Flutter]: a [Widget] object is IMMUABLE (rebuilt on every render, like a simple configuration object), whereas its associated [State] remains the same SURVIT from one render to the next.

docs.title: 4.5. Sharing state between widgets: provider, the equivalent of provide/inject
docs.text:
[Vue.js] shares state between remote components via the pair [provide]/[inject]; [React] uses a [Context]; [Angular] is an injectable singleton service. [Flutter] does not have any of these mechanisms built into the framework itself: the third-party package [provider] (see [pubspec.yaml], Chapter 4), which is virtually indispensable in the [Flutter] ecosystem, serves this purpose. Its principle: a [ChangeNotifier] class (a standard [Dart] class, which can notify its listeners of a change via [notifyListeners()]) is made available to an entire subtree of widgets by a [ChangeNotifierProvider] placed at its root (see [MultiProvider] in [lib/main.dart], which is equivalent to the [app.provide(clé, valeur)] calls on the [Vue.js] side); any descendant widget then re-reads it using [context.watch<MonService>()] (subscribes to future changes—the equivalent of [useXxx()] on the [Vue.js] side) or [context.read<MonService>()] (one-time read, without resubscription—a distinction that [Vue.js] does not need to make).

Key difference from [reactive(...)]: a [ChangeNotifier] does not automatically detect RIEN. [reactive(...)] wraps an object in a [JavaScript] proxy that intercepts every LECTURE and every ÉCRITURE property; a [ChangeNotifier] [Dart] is a regular class, and it is up to the developer to explicitly call [notifyListeners()] after every modification that should trigger a new rendering—requiring more manual discipline, in exchange for a mechanism that doesn’t rely on “magic” proxies to understand.

docs.title: 4.6. No separate template language: conditional rendering and lists
docs.text: [v-if]/[v-else] and [v-for] ([Vue.js]) — such as [@if]/[@for] on the [Angular] side, or the ternary operators && and [.map(...)] on the [React] side - are converted, in [Flutter], back into [Dart] and ORDINAIRES expressions, directly within [build(...)]: a [if]/classic [else] and [Dart] for a condition, and [.map((element) => Widget(...)).toList()] for a list—the same concept as [.map(...)] on the [React] side, since [Flutter], like [React], does not recognize a separate “template language” distinct from the programming language itself. The [if (condition) ...[ WidgetA, WidgetB ]] syntax (“if collection,” used for example in [lib/app.dart], Chapter 4) takes this logic a step further than [React]: a CONDITION inserted directly within a literal list of widgets, without a ternary operator or intermediate function.

docs.title: 4.7. Dart: a close cousin of TypeScript, not JavaScript
docs.text:
[Dart] was never intended as an alternative to [TypeScript] for the web (unlike the latter, which was specifically designed as a superset of [JavaScript]): it is an independent language, typed as STATIQUEMENT from the outset (no implicit “[any]” mode), compiled—never interpreted as-is. For a developer coming from [TypeScript] (like the three previous variants in this course), the essentials translate almost directly: classes, interfaces ([Dart] uses [abstract class] or simple implemented classes, rather than a separate [interface] keyword), generics ([Reponse<T>], see Chapter 4), [async]/[await] on [Future<T>] (the EXACT equivalent of [Promise<T>] and [TypeScript]), and a nullability check built into the type system ([String?] rather than a string that is always present—the equivalent of the [strict] mode of [TypeScript], but enforced by the language itself rather than by a compiler option).

A notable difference, encountered in every file in the following chapter that decodes JSON ([core/models/rdv_models.dart]): [TypeScript] removes its types at compile time—a [interface] is checked only at compile time, a decoded JSON object is then used as TEL and QUEL at runtime ([JSON.parse(...) as Reponse<T>], a simple promise made to the compiler). [Dart], on the other hand, has its types determined at runtime: GARDE always returns dynamic types ([Map<String, dynamic>]), which must be explicitly converted to class instances using a hand-written [fromJson(...)] constructor—more verbose at first, but a missing key or one of an unexpected type then raises an immediate and clear exception, rather than propagating silently.

docs.title: 4.8. A first minimal example
docs.text:
Here is the smallest [Flutter] application that displays something on the screen—compare this with [lib/main.dart]/[lib/app.dart] from Chapter 4, which are significantly more feature-rich but built using the same building blocks as EXACTEMENT ([runApp(...)], [MaterialApp], and a root widget).

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';

void main() {
  runApp(
    const MaterialApp(
      home: Scaffold(
        body: Center(child: Text('Bonjour, RdvMedecins !')),
      ),
    ),
  );
}

Let's go over this code:

  • Line 1: [import 'package:flutter/material.dart';] — equivalent to [import { ... } from 'vue']: [material.dart] includes all the “Material Design” widgets ([Google]) used in this document—buttons, text fields, app bars, etc. [Flutter] also offers a set of [Cupertino] widgets (with the [iOS] style), which are not used in this course, for those who prefer this style on mobile devices ([Apple]).
  • Line 3: [void main() {] — the entry point of a program [Dart], EXACTEMENT, just like that of a program [C]/[Java] - [Flutter] has no equivalent to the [HTML] of a web page, into which a [main.ts] script would then be embedded: the application launches ICI directly.
  • Line 4: [runApp(...)] — starts the rendering engine [Flutter] and provides it with the root widget to display—the equivalent of [createApp(App).mount('#app')] on the [Vue.js] ([src/main.ts]), in a single call rather than two.
  • lines 5–9: [MaterialApp(home: Scaffold(body: Center(...)))] — a ARBRE of nested widgets, each with a specific responsibility: [MaterialApp] configures the theme and navigation; [Scaffold] provides the standard screen structure (area for an application bar, content area, etc.); [Center] centers its child; [Text] displays a string. None of these four widgets is a special case of the language: they are simply CLASSES and [Dart], like the ones this course will write itself in the next chapter.

docs.title: 4.9. Summary: Angular -> React -> Vue.js -> Flutter
docs.text:
See also the [README.md] included with the code for this chapter for the full version.

  • [Angular] components / [.vue] files / [.tsx] files → [Widgets] [Dart] ([StatelessWidget]/[StatefulWidget])
  • [signal()]/[ref()]/[useState()] → mutable fields + [setState(...)] (local state), [ChangeNotifier] (shared state)
  • [input()]/[output()], [defineProps]/[defineEmits], function properties → constructor parameters (inputs), functions passed as parameters (outputs)
  • injectable/composable services + [provide]/[inject]/[Context] → service classes + package [provider]
  • separate template [Angular], [<template>], [Vue.js], [JSX], [React] → method [build(BuildContext)] (pure Dart)
  • [HttpClient]/[fetch] → package [http]
  • [localStorage] → [shared_preferences]
  • No router (single-screen application, in all 5 variants of this course)

docs.title: 5. Chapter 4 - The Flutter client for the RdvMedecins application
5.1. Architecture Overview
docs.text: This client communicates with the course’s [rdvmedecins-nestjs-server] server—which remains strictly unchanged—via the same routes (HTTP) already documented (POST, [/login], GET, [/getAllMedecins], GET [/getAllClients], GET [/getAgendaMedecinJour/:idMedecin/:jour], POST [/ajouterRv], POST [/supprimerRv]), with the same envelope JSON [{ status, data }] and the same token-based authentication [JWT] (header [Authorization: Bearer <jeton>]). For this variant, the overall architecture gains a third component: depending on the chosen compilation target (see Chapter 5), it is no longer just a browser that executes the client, but potentially a mobile or desktop operating system that directly executes the compiled code [Dart]—the server [NestJS], meanwhile, still only processes the same requests HTTP, regardless of the target.

docs.text:
rdvmedecins_flutter_client/
├── pubspec.yaml                      configuration du projet (dépendances, assets)
├── assets/
│   └── i18n/                         dictionnaires de traduction (fr.json, en.json)
└── lib/

docs.title: 5.4.1. lib/main.dart
docs.text:
Porting [src/main.ts] (client [Vue.js]): builds this client's services, makes them available to the entire widget tree via [provider], and then starts the application.

// Vue.js from this course: this file explicitly starts the application
// (runApp(...) here; createApp(...).mount(...) on the Vue.js side) ET the
// configuration.
//
// Vue.js configures its application with app.provide(key, value), called
// directly on the application instance—Flutter/provider uses
// a widget, MultiProvider, placed at the root of the tree (see runApp(...)
// below): each ChangeNotifierProvider/Provider it contains makes
// makes the subtree it encloses available to TOUT, exactly
// just as app.provide(...) did for all descendant components—
// the same idea, expressed as a WIDGET rather than as a call to

// the configuration of a shared state).
//

// on the Vue.js side: AuthService(settings) requires that `settings` already exists
// (to read apiBaseUrl); RdvService requires authHttp ET from "settings."
//
// DIFFÉRENCE IMPORTANTE with Vue.js: createAuthStore(settings) and
// creerLanguageStore() on the Vue.js side read SYNCHRONEMENT localStorage
// during their construction, even before the first render. Their
// Flutter equivalents (AuthService.init(), TranslationsService.init())
// are ASYNCHRONES (see their respective files): main() itself must
// therefore become an async function, and ATTENDRE (await) these two
// initializations AVANT must call runApp(...)—otherwise, the first screen
// displayed would ignore any session or language already stored, the
// while shared_preferences responds.
//
// Like the Angular, React, and Vue.js clients in this course (single-page,
// no routing table), this Flutter client does not use QUE the
// minimal navigation provided by MaterialApp (required for showDialog(), see
// features/booking_dialog/booking_dialog.dart): AppRoot (see app.dart)
//displays either the login screen or the rest of the application, depending on
// AuthService.estConnecte—a simple Dart if/else statement is sufficient; a
// routing package (go_router or another) would not have added anything to a single-screen application
// with a single screen.
// =========================================================================

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';
import 'package:provider/provider.dart';

import 'app.dart';
import 'core/http/auth_http_client.dart';
import 'core/i18n/translations_service.dart';
import 'core/services/auth_service.dart';
import 'core/services/rdv_service.dart';
import 'core/services/settings_service.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  // WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized(): essential as soon as
  // calls a API Flutter AVANT runApp(...) (here, shared_preferences and
  // rootBundle.loadString(...) in TranslationsService.init()) - without
  // this line, these calls would fail on startup. Vue.js is in no way
  // comparable: the browser is always “ready” even before
  // src/main.ts runs.
  WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized();

  // 1. SettingsService first: AuthService and RdvService depend on it
  // (apiBaseUrl).
  final settings = SettingsService();

  // 2. AuthService: receives settings directly from the manufacturer, such as
  // creerAuthStore (settingsStore) on the Vue.js side - then init() restores a
  // any cached session (see the header comment
  // above regarding the asynchronous nature of this step).
  final auth = AuthService(settings);
  await auth.init();

  // 3. the authenticated HTTP layer, then the business service—both
  // constructed ICI, just once, rather than inside a widget
  // (where they would be rebuilt with each render): exactly the same
  // principle as creerSettingsStore()/creerAuthStore(...), called a
  // only once before app.mount(...) on the Vue.js side.
  final authHttp = AuthHttpClient(auth);
  final rdv = RdvService(authHttp, settings);

  // 4. TranslationsService: loads the startup dictionary (the
  // stored language, or French by default) - AUCUNE dependency
  // order dependency with the previous steps (unlike
  // creerLanguageStore() on the Vue.js side, which had to wait
  // app.use(i18n): this file reimplements everything itself; see
  // core/i18n/translations_service.dart, so there is no
  // third-party plugin to install before you can use it).
  final translations = TranslationsService();
  await translations.init();

  runApp(
    // MultiProvider: combines multiple providers into a single widget,
    // rather than nesting them manually (Provider(...) > Provider(...)
    // > Provider(...) > ...)—resulting in readability comparable to the following
    // of calls like "app.provide(SettingsKey, ...); app.provide(AuthKey, ...);
    // app.provide(LanguageKey, ...);" on the Vue.js side, despite the difference in
    // form (a list of widgets rather than a sequence of instructions).
    MultiProvider(
      providers: [
        // .value(...) rather than Provider(create: ...): these instances
        // already exist (constructed above)—.value(...) simply makes them
        // simply available to the widget tree, without creating
        // new ones. ChangeNotifierProvider, specifically, subscribes
        // notifyListeners() and automatically redraws any
        // widget that has called context.watch<...>() on this provider (see
        // lib/app.dart) — the role played by the “reactive” nature of a
        // reactive(...) on the Vue.js side.
        ChangeNotifierProvider.value(value: settings),
        ChangeNotifierProvider.value(value: auth),
        ChangeNotifierProvider.value(value: translations),
        // RdvService is not PAS a ChangeNotifier (nothing in this service
        // does not change over time once it has been constructed): a simple Provider
        // is sufficient; it simply makes this instance available, without
        // any concept of notification.
        Provider.value(value: rdv),
      ],
      child: const RdvMedecinsApp(),
    ),
  );
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 60: [WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized();] — required whenever you call a API, [Flutter], AVANT, or [runApp(...)] (here, [shared_preferences] and [rootBundle.loadString(...)])—without this line, these calls would fail at startup; [Vue.js] has nothing of the sort to anticipate, since the browser is always “ready” even before [src/main.ts] is executed.
  • Lines 70–71: [final auth = AuthService(settings); await auth.init();] — DIFFÉRENCE MAJEURE with [creerAuthStore(settingsStore)] on the side of [Vue.js], which reads [localStorage] SYNCHRONEMENT as soon as it is built: [AuthService.init()] is explicitly [async], and [main()] itself must therefore be the same in order to be able to ATTENDRE before [runApp(...)] — otherwise, the first screen displayed would ignore a session already stored in memory while waiting for [shared_preferences] to respond.
  • Line 89: [await translations.init();] — same note as above regarding the stored language; unlike [creerLanguageStore()] relative to [Vue.js], which had to wait for [app.use(i18n)], this step has no sequential dependency on the previous ones: [TranslationsService] reimplements everything on its own, without requiring any third-party plugins to be installed beforehand.
  • Lines 98–116: [MultiProvider(providers: [...], child: const RdvMedecinsApp())] — the equivalent, in the form of WIDGET rather than imperative calls, of the sequence [app.provide(SettingsKey, ...); app.provide(AuthKey, ...); app.provide(LanguageKey, ...);] on the [Vue.js] side: Each [ChangeNotifierProvider.value(...)] makes a pre-built instance available to the entire subtree.

docs.title: 5.4.2. lib/app.dart
docs.text:
Porting [src/app/App.vue]: the RACINE widget from the application (constructed by [lib/main.dart])—the “conductor” that holds the business state and responds to actions from the [lib/features/] widgets, and the authentication “guard.”

// =========================================================================
// app.dart
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Port of src/app/App.vue (the Vue.js client from this course): the widget
// RACINE widget of the application (built by lib/main.dart). As in the
// three other variants in this course, it acts as the “orchestra conductor”
// "conductor": it maintains the application state (doctors, clients,
// displayed calendar, last doctor/day searched for...) and responds to actions
// from the "business logic" widgets in lib/features/ to call the server NestJS at the
// right time, via RdvService.
//
// Since authentication was added, this widget also acts as a
// "guard": as long as AuthService.estConnecte is false, it displays only
// LoginPage (see lib/features/login/); since all server routes are
// protected by JwtAuthGuard, it would be pointless anyway (and a source
// 401 errors) to load doctors/clients/calendar before logging in.
//
// Two classes, as in the other “stateful” files for this client:
// RdvMedecinsApp (the MaterialApp—the root ABSOLUE, see lib/main.dart) and
// AppRoot/_AppRootState (the actual equivalent of App.vue, with its entire state).
// =========================================================================

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';
import 'package:provider/provider.dart';

import 'core/i18n/translations_service.dart';
import 'core/models/rdv_models.dart';
import 'core/services/auth_service.dart';
import 'core/services/rdv_service.dart';
import 'core/services/settings_service.dart';
import 'features/agenda/agenda_view.dart';
import 'features/booking_dialog/booking_dialog.dart';
import 'features/doctor_day_picker/doctor_day_picker.dart';
import 'features/login/login_page.dart';

// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// RdvMedecinsApp: the Flutter root in the strict sense—MaterialApp provides
// the theme and navigation (Navigator, used by showDialog(), see
// features/booking_dialog/booking_dialog.dart) and system translations
// (scrolling, dialog boxes...). This is roughly
// roughly equivalent to what index.html + the app.mount('#app')
// together on the Vue.js side (src/main.ts)—except that here, this
// "placeholder" is itself part of the application’s Dart code, rather
// than a separate HTML file.
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
class RdvMedecinsApp extends StatelessWidget {
  const RdvMedecinsApp({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return MaterialApp(
      debugShowCheckedModeBanner: false,
      // appBarTheme explicitly: the default Material 3 theme gives
      // AppBar a light background (colorScheme.surface)—to restore the
      // blue banner with white text for "navbar navbar-dark bg-primary" on the
      // Vue.js (see App.vue), here we explicitly set the background and text,
      // rather than hard-coding a text color for each Text()
      // in AppRoot below (see auth.nom, further down)—a
      // single source of truth for the banner's appearance.
      theme: ThemeData(
        colorSchemeSeed: Colors.blue,
        useMaterial3: true,
        appBarTheme: const AppBarTheme(
          backgroundColor: Colors.blue,
          foregroundColor: Colors.white,
        ),
      ),
      home: const AppRoot(),
    );
  }
}

class AppRoot extends StatefulWidget {
  const AppRoot({super.key});

  @override
  State<AppRoot> createState() => _AppRootState();
}

class _AppRootState extends State<AppRoot> {
  // --- application status ---------------------------------------------
  // the direct equivalent of the ref(...) fields in App.vue, in the form of simple
  // mutable fields from _AppRootState: setState(...) (see the methods
  // below) serves as a substitute for the automatic responsiveness of Vue.js.
  List<Medecin> _medecins = [];
  List<Client> _clients = [];
  AgendaMedecinJour? _agenda;
  String? _erreur;

  // saves the last search (doctor + day) so that
  // refresh the calendar after a booking or cancellation—even
  // regardless of whether it’s on the dernierIdMedecin/dernierJour side or the Vue.js side.
  int? _dernierIdMedecin;
  String? _dernierJour;

  // permanent reference to AuthService, to be able to
  // unsubscribe properly in `dispose()` (see below) — see the
  // comment on initState() below for the reason behind this choice.
  late final AuthService _auth;

  @override
  void initState() {
    super.initState();
    // context.read<AuthService>() : When initState() runs, the
    // widget is already correctly inserted into the tree (unlike the
    // constructor, where `context` is not yet usable for
    // dependency injection)—but we’re using PAS context.watch(...)
    // here: a StatefulWidget should subscribe to a provider only once
    // time, explicitly, and never inside initState() with watch()
    // (which assumes a build context). We therefore keep the reference in
    // a field (_auth) and subscribe ourselves using addListener(...).
    _auth = context.read<AuthService>();
    _auth.addListener(_onAuthChange);

    // equivalent to "watch(() => auth.estConnecte, ..., { immediate: true })"
    // On the Vue.js side: { immediate: true } triggers IMMÉDIATEMENT the
    // callback, without waiting for the first change—useful if a session
    // was already stored (see AuthService.init(), expected by
    // lib/main.dart before runApp(...)). Vue.js offers this option
    // directly; Flutter does not have an equivalent mechanism built into
    // addListener(...), so we replicate the same effect at LA MAIN: an
    // explicit call immediately after the subscription, in addition to the subscription
    // itself.
    if (_auth.estConnecte) {
      _chargerListesInitiales();
    }
  }

  @override
  void dispose() {
    // to unsubscribe is INDISPENSABLE here: without this, _onAuthChange
    // would continue to be called after this widget is destroyed (by
    // for example, during a hot reload or a route change), and
    // would throw an exception on the first call to setState(...) on a widget
    // that has been unmounted. Vue.js has nothing comparable to worry about: watch(...) is
    // automatically “cleaned up” when the component that created it is destroyed.
    _auth.removeListener(_onAuthChange);
    super.dispose();
  }

  void _onAuthChange() {
    if (_auth.estConnecte) {
      _chargerListesInitiales();
    }
  }

  // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  // when a user logs in (successful login, or session
  // restored from shared_preferences), it is loaded once and for all
  // all lists of doctors and clients.
  // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  void _chargerListesInitiales() {
    final rdv = context.read<RdvService>();
    rdv.getAllMedecins().then((resultat) {
      if (mounted) setState(() => _medecins = resultat);
    }).catchError((Object err) {
      if (mounted) setState(() => _erreur = err.toString());
    });
    rdv.getAllClients().then((resultat) {
      if (mounted) setState(() => _clients = resultat);
    }).catchError((Object err) {
      if (mounted) setState(() => _erreur = err.toString());
    });
  }

  // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  // responds to the "Log Out" button: clears the ET business state
  // is displayed—otherwise, a new user logging in afterward
  // would briefly see the previous user’s calendar.
  // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  Future<void> _onDeconnexion() async {
    await _auth.seDeconnecter();
    setState(() {
      _medecins = [];
      _clients = [];
      _agenda = null;
      _erreur = null;
      _dernierIdMedecin = null;
      _dernierJour = null;
    });
  }

  // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  // responds to the call from onRechercher(...) of the widget DoctorDayPicker
  // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  void _onRechercherAgenda(int idMedecin, String jour) {
    setState(() {
      _erreur = null;
      _dernierIdMedecin = idMedecin;
      _dernierJour = jour;
    });
    _chargerAgenda();
  }

  // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  // responds to the call from onReserver(...) from the widget AgendaView: ICI,
  // unlike Vue.js (which simply opened the window by
  // and storing creneauEnReservation), we open the
  // dialog box with showDialog (via ouvrirBookingDialog(...)) and we get ATTEND
  // its result—see the header of booking_dialog.dart for details on
  // this structural difference.
  // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  Future<void> _onDemandeReservation(CreneauJson creneau) async {
    final dernierJour = _dernierJour;
    if (dernierJour == null) {
      return;
    }
    final idClient = await ouvrirBookingDialog(context: context, creneau: creneau, clients: _clients);
    if (idClient == null) {
      return; // The user closed the dialog box without selecting a patient
    }
    try {
      await context.read<RdvService>().ajouterRv(dernierJour, idClient, creneau.id);
      _chargerAgenda(); // The calendar is refreshed: the time slot now appears as booked
    } catch (err) {
      if (mounted) setState(() => _erreur = err.toString());
    }
  }

  // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  // responds to the call from onAnnuler(...) by the widget AgendaView
  // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  Future<void> _onAnnulerRv(RvJson rv) async {
    try {
      await context.read<RdvService>().supprimerRv(rv.id);
      _chargerAgenda(); // The calendar is refreshed: the time slot is now available again
    } catch (err) {
      if (mounted) setState(() => _erreur = err.toString());
    }
  }

  void _chargerAgenda() {
    final idMedecin = _dernierIdMedecin;
    final jour = _dernierJour;
    if (idMedecin == null || jour == null) {
      return;
    }
    context.read<RdvService>().getAgendaMedecinJour(idMedecin, jour).then((resultat) {
      if (mounted) setState(() => _agenda = resultat);
    }).catchError((Object err) {
      if (mounted) setState(() => _erreur = err.toString());
    });
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    // context.watch<...>() on the TROIS providers whose display depends on it
    // directly: each call subscribes this widget to future changes to
    // this provider—if one of them notifies (notifyListeners()), build(...)
    // is automatically called again. This is the mechanism that
    // replaces, in this case, the automatic responsiveness of Vue.js mentioned in
    // core/services/settings_service.dart.
    final t = context.watch<TranslationsService>().t;
    final langue = context.watch<TranslationsService>();
    final auth = context.watch<AuthService>();
    final settings = context.watch<SettingsService>();
    // narrow screen (phone in portrait mode): the title bar is simplified
    // (see actions: below), due to lack of space to display everything that
    // easily fits on a wide screen.
    final etroit = MediaQuery.sizeOf(context).width < 600;

    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(
        title: Text(t('APP.TITLE')),
        actions: [
          // FR/EN selector: TOUJOURS visible (including on the
          // login screen)—the counterpart to the <div class="btn-group"> always
          // displayed on the App.vue side.
          SegmentedButton<String>(
            segments: const [
              ButtonSegment(value: 'fr', label: Text('FR')),
              ButtonSegment(value: 'en', label: Text('EN')),
            ],
            selected: {langue.langueCourante},
            onSelectionChanged: (choix) => langue.changerLangue(choix.first),
            showSelectedIcon: false,
          ),
          const SizedBox(width: 12),
          // The role badge, name, and logout button, however,
          // appear only once logged in (auth.estConnecte)—even
          // provided that the <template v-if="auth.estConnecte"> from App.vue.
          if (auth.estConnecte) ...[
            Chip(label: Text(auth.role?.versChaine() ?? '')),
            const SizedBox(width: 8),
            // no hard-coded color style here: this Text() inherits the
            // foregroundColor white set to appBarTheme (see RdvMedecinsApp
            // above), just like "navbar-dark" in Bootstrap
            // which colored all its content white by default.
            // on a narrow screen, the name is hidden: the role badge and the
            // logout button are sufficient, and the title bar fits within the width.
            if (!etroit) Text(auth.nom ?? ''),
            IconButton(
              tooltip: t('APP.LOGOUT'),
              icon: const Icon(Icons.logout),
              onPressed: _onDeconnexion,
            ),
          ],
          const SizedBox(width: 8),
        ],
      ),
      body: SafeArea(
        child: SingleChildScrollView(
          padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
          child: Column(
            crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.start,
            children: [
              // URL from the server: useful both before and after logging in
              // — displayed in a small, dedicated private widget, _ServerUrlField
              // (see below), for the reasons explained next to its
              // definition.
              ConstrainedBox(
                constraints: const BoxConstraints(maxWidth: 320),
                child: _ServerUrlField(settings: settings, label: t('APP.SERVER_URL_LABEL')),
              ),
              const SizedBox(height: 16),

              if (_erreur != null) ...[
                Container(
                  width: double.infinity,
                  padding: const EdgeInsets.all(12),
                  decoration: BoxDecoration(
                    color: Theme.of(context).colorScheme.errorContainer,
                    borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(4),
                  ),
                  child: Text(
                    _erreur!,
                    style: TextStyle(color: Theme.of(context).colorScheme.onErrorContainer),
                  ),
                ),
                const SizedBox(height: 16),
              ],

              // not logged in: nothing but the login screen—
              // the exact equivalent of "<Login v-if="!auth.estConnecte" />"
              // on the Vue.js side.
              if (!auth.estConnecte)
                const LoginPage()
              else ...[
                // Widget 1: Select doctor and date
                DoctorDayPicker(medecins: _medecins, onRechercher: _onRechercherAgenda),
                const SizedBox(height: 16),
                // Widget 2: Calendar view - peutModifier form
                // "Book"/"Cancel" for a role USER
                AgendaView(
                  agenda: _agenda,
                  peutModifier: auth.estAdmin,
                  onReserver: _onDemandeReservation,
                  onAnnuler: _onAnnulerRv,
                ),
              ],
            ],
          ),
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}

// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// _ServerUrlField: a small StatefulWidget PRIVÉ dedicated to the "URL of the
// server." On the Vue.js side, this field fits on a single line, directly
// in the <template> of App.vue (<input v-model="settings.apiBaseUrl">):
// v-model handles the synchronization between the field
// and settings.apiBaseUrl. Flutter does not have a bidirectional binding
// built into TextField (see lib/features/login/login_page.dart): it
// requires a TextEditingController, and therefore an owner capable of creating it
// and release it (initState/dispose)—a TEXTE ÉDITABLE linked to a
// provider cannot simply be a PAS in Flutter,
// unlike an equivalent Vue.js field, which does not require any
// separate “component” to exist.
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
class _ServerUrlField extends StatefulWidget {
  final SettingsService settings;
  final String label;

  const _ServerUrlField({required this.settings, required this.label});

  @override
  State<_ServerUrlField> createState() => _ServerUrlFieldState();
}

class _ServerUrlFieldState extends State<_ServerUrlField> {
  late final TextEditingController _controller;

  @override
  void initState() {
    super.initState();
    _controller = TextEditingController(text: widget.settings.apiBaseUrl);
  }

  @override
  void dispose() {
    _controller.dispose();
    super.dispose();
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return TextField(
      controller: _controller,
      decoration: InputDecoration(labelText: widget.label, isDense: true),
      // onChanged rather than onSubmitted: each keystroke is reflected
      // immediately to SettingsService, exactly as
      // v-model on the Vue.js side for each character typed (not just upon
      // form submission).
      onChanged: widget.settings.setApiBaseUrl,
    );
  }
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • lines 46–71: [class RdvMedecinsApp extends StatelessWidget] — the root [Flutter] in the strict sense: [MaterialApp] provides the theme and navigation (essential for [showDialog(...)], see [booking_dialog.dart] below) — roughly equivalent to what [index.html] + [app.mount('#app')] did together on the [Vue.js] side.
  • lines 60–66: [appBarTheme: const AppBarTheme(backgroundColor: Colors.blue, foregroundColor: Colors.white)] — replicates the appearance of ["navbar navbar-dark bg-primary"] ([Bootstrap], see [App.vue]): A default [Material 3] theme would give [AppBar] a light background, so it must be explicitly set to restore the familiar blue banner with white text.
  • lines 96–127: [initState()] — duplicated, to LA MAIN, the equivalent of [watch(() => auth.estConnecte, ..., { immediate: true })] on the [Vue.js] side (see [App.vue]): [Flutter] does not have the [immediate] option embedded in [addListener(...)], so you must subscribe to PUIS to explicitly check the current status once—two steps where [Vue.js] requires only one.
  • Lines 129–139: [dispose() { _auth.removeListener(_onAuthChange); }] — INDISPENSABLE: Without this unsubscription, [_onAuthChange] would continue to be called after the widget is destroyed and would cause an exception on the first call to [setState(...)] on a dismantled widget. [Vue.js] has nothing comparable to anticipate, as [watch(...)] is automatically “cleaned up” when the component that created it is destroyed.
  • Lines 203–218: [_onDemandeReservation(...)] — LA is the most visible structural difference in this entire client: rather than opening a “window” by storing a Boolean state (see [creneauEnReservation] on the [Vue.js] side), this widget [await] directly displays the result of [ouvrirBookingDialog(...)]—see the full comment in [booking_dialog.dart], later in this chapter.
  • Lines 253–256: four [context.watch<...>()] at the beginning of [build(...)]—this widget automatically redraws as soon as any one of these four services (IMPORTE or LEQUEL) notifies a change ([notifyListeners()]), exactly the role played by the automatic responsiveness of [Vue.js] for [auth], [settings], and [langue] in [App.vue].
  • Lines 260 and 291: [MediaQuery.sizeOf(context).width < 600] — the screen (or window) width is used to make the title bar lighter on a phone in portrait mode: the user’s name is hidden ([if (!etroit) Text(...)], a simple [if] Dart in the middle of a list of widgets), while the role badge and the logout button remain visible. On line 276, [showSelectedIcon: false] removes the checkmark that [SegmentedButton] adds to the selected option, which unnecessarily widened the [FR]/[EN] selector. Without these two adjustments, the [actions:] elements of the [AppBar] exceed the width of a phone in portrait orientation.
  • Lines 359–409: [class _ServerUrlField] — a small [StatefulWidget] PRIVÉ dedicated to the “URL from the server” field. As for [Vue.js], this field fit on a single line ([<input v-model="settings.apiBaseUrl">]): [Flutter] does not have a bidirectional link integrated with [TextField], so a [TextEditingController] is required, along with an owner capable of creating or releasing it—an editable text linked to a provider cannot simply be a [StatelessWidget] in [Flutter].

docs.title: 5.5.1. lib/core/models/rdv_models.dart
docs.text:
Port of [core/models/rdv.models.ts], itself copied verbatim from the clients [Angular] and [React]: the classes that describe the format of the JSON data exchanged with the server, with no dependencies on [Flutter]—the “pure” [Dart].

// =========================================================================
// core/models/rdv_models.dart
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Port of core/models/rdv.models.ts (the Vue.js client from this course),
// which is copied verbatim from the Angular and React clients: the Dart classes that
// describe the format of the data JSON received from the server NestJS. Like their
// counterparts TypeScript, these classes do not depend on any framework UI
// framework (no Flutter imports here)—it’s “pure” Dart, just like
// rdv.models.ts was "pure" TypeScript.
//
// DIFFÉRENCE STRUCTURELLE with TypeScript: a "interface" TypeScript is
// a simple description of FORME, verified only at compile time—
// at runtime, a decoded JSON object (JSON.parse) is used TEL QUEL,
// without conversion, and TypeScript “trusts” the developer (see
// "as Response<T>" from rdv.service.ts). Dart does not have this concept of typing
// implicit structural typing: jsonDecode(...) always returns
// dynamic types (Map<String, dynamic>, List<dynamic>...), which must be
// must be explicitly converted to Dart class instances using a constructor
// fromJson(...)—which is present in CHACUNE for the classes below. It’s more
// verbose to write once, but the conversion is verified at runtime
// (a missing key or one of the wrong type immediately raises an explicit exception
// ), whereas incorrect typing TypeScript might go unnoticed.
// =========================================================================

// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// a common wrapper for all server responses (see Reponse<T> on the
// NestJS, and the client’s Reponse<T> interface Vue.js).
//
// Dart also generalizes using angle brackets (<T>), exactly like
// TypeScript—the main difference is that here, we cannot simply use
// an “as T” to convert the field [data]: you must provide the function
// that knows how to construct a T from raw JSON (the parameter
// [parseData] below), because Dart does not know T at runtime
// (type erasure prevents writing "T.fromJson(...)"
// directly).
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
class Reponse<T> {
  final int status; // 0 = success, anything else = failure (see StatutReponse on the server side)
  final T? data;

  Reponse({required this.status, required this.data});

  factory Reponse.fromJson(
    Map<String, dynamic> json,
    T Function(dynamic donneesBrutes) parseData,
  ) {
    final donneesBrutes = json['data'];
    return Reponse<T>(
      status: json['status'] as int,
      data: donneesBrutes == null ? null : parseData(donneesBrutes),
    );
  }
}

class Medecin {
  final int id;
  final String titre;
  final String nom;
  final String prenom;

  Medecin({required this.id, required this.titre, required this.nom, required this.prenom});

  factory Medecin.fromJson(Map<String, dynamic> json) => Medecin(
        id: json['id'] as int,
        titre: json['titre'] as String,
        nom: json['nom'] as String,
        prenom: json['prenom'] as String,
      );
}

// [Client] refers here to a PATIENT from the medical practice (business domain vocabulary, inherited from the
// business domain, inherited from the original document)—not to be confused with
// "client HTTP," nor with this Flutter client itself!
class Client {
  final int id;
  final String titre;
  final String nom;
  final String prenom;

  Client({required this.id, required this.titre, required this.nom, required this.prenom});

  factory Client.fromJson(Map<String, dynamic> json) => Client(
        id: json['id'] as int,
        titre: json['titre'] as String,
        nom: json['nom'] as String,
        prenom: json['prenom'] as String,
      );
}

// "light" form of a time slot, as returned by the server
// (see getMapForCreneau on the NestJS side): only the fields needed for display.
class CreneauJson {
  final int id;
  final int hDebut;
  final int mDebut;
  final int hFin;
  final int mFin;

  CreneauJson({
    required this.id,
    required this.hDebut,
    required this.mDebut,
    required this.hFin,
    required this.mFin,
  });

  factory CreneauJson.fromJson(Map<String, dynamic> json) => CreneauJson(
        id: json['id'] as int,
        hDebut: json['hDebut'] as int,
        mDebut: json['mDebut'] as int,
        hFin: json['hFin'] as int,
        mFin: json['mFin'] as int,
      );
}

// "light" format of an appointment (see getMapForRv on the NestJS side)
class RvJson {
  final int id;
  final String jour; // "yyyy-MM-dd" format
  final Client? client;
  final CreneauJson? creneau;

  RvJson({required this.id, required this.jour, required this.client, required this.creneau});

  factory RvJson.fromJson(Map<String, dynamic> json) => RvJson(
        id: json['id'] as int,
        jour: json['jour'] as String,
        client: json['client'] == null ? null : Client.fromJson(json['client'] as Map<String, dynamic>),
        creneau: json['creneau'] == null ? null : CreneauJson.fromJson(json['creneau'] as Map<String, dynamic>),
      );
}

// a slot in a doctor’s schedule, either available (rv == null) or booked
class CreneauAgenda {
  final CreneauJson creneau;
  final RvJson? rv;

  CreneauAgenda({required this.creneau, required this.rv});

  factory CreneauAgenda.fromJson(Map<String, dynamic> json) => CreneauAgenda(
        creneau: CreneauJson.fromJson(json['creneau'] as Map<String, dynamic>),
        rv: json['rv'] == null ? null : RvJson.fromJson(json['rv'] as Map<String, dynamic>),
      );
}

// a doctor’s full schedule for a given day (see GET /getAgendaMedecinJour/:idMedecin/:day)
class AgendaMedecinJour {
  final Medecin medecin;
  final String jour;
  final List<CreneauAgenda> creneaux;

  AgendaMedecinJour({required this.medecin, required this.jour, required this.creneaux});

  factory AgendaMedecinJour.fromJson(Map<String, dynamic> json) => AgendaMedecinJour(
        medecin: Medecin.fromJson(json['medecin'] as Map<String, dynamic>),
        jour: json['jour'] as String,
        creneaux: (json['creneaux'] as List<dynamic>)
            .map((e) => CreneauAgenda.fromJson(e as Map<String, dynamic>))
            .toList(),
      );
}

// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// authentication (see server: src/auth/, specifically login-resultat.model.ts)
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------

// the only two roles managed by the application—exact copy of the type
// [Role] from the server (src/entities/user.entity.ts). Where TypeScript
// is simply a union of strings ('ADMIN' | 'USER'), Dart has a
// true concept of enumeration (enum): more secure (impossible to generate an
// accidentally create a Role other than these two values), at the cost of a small round-trip
// back-and-forth with the string JSON ("ADMIN"/"USER") via
// depuisChaine(...)/versChaine() below—a TypeScript "Role type =
// 'ADMIN' | 'USER'" requires no conversion, a string JSON EST
// is already a valid value of that type.
enum Role {
  admin,
  user;

  static Role depuisChaine(String valeur) {
    switch (valeur) {
      case 'ADMIN':
        return Role.admin;
      case 'USER':
        return Role.user;
      default:
        throw ArgumentError('Rôle inconnu : $valeur');
    }
  }

  String versChaine() => this == Role.admin ? 'ADMIN' : 'USER';
}

// is the data returned by POST /login (in the usual Reponse<T> envelope)
class LoginResultat {
  final String accessToken;
  final String login;
  final String nom;
  final Role role;

  LoginResultat({required this.accessToken, required this.login, required this.nom, required this.role});

  factory LoginResultat.fromJson(Map<String, dynamic> json) => LoginResultat(
        accessToken: json['accessToken'] as String,
        login: json['login'] as String,
        nom: json['nom'] as String,
        role: Role.depuisChaine(json['role'] as String),
      );
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • Lines 11–22: The header comment details the key structural difference in this file—a [interface] [TypeScript] is only checked against the COMPILATION; [Dart] GARDE its types at runtime, hence an explicit [fromJson(...)] constructor on each class (absent from [rdv.models.ts]).
  • Lines 37–53: [class Reponse<T>] and its factory [fromJson(json, parseData)]—receives a FONCTION ([parseData]) rather than relying on a simple [as Reponse<T>] as the [TypeScript] side (see [rdv.service.ts]): [Dart] does not know [T] at runtime (type erasure), so it cannot write [T.fromJson(...)] itself.
  • Lines 71–73: The comment notes that [Client] refers to a PATIENT from the medical practice (business domain vocabulary)—not to be confused with “client HTTP,” nor with this client [Flutter] itself, an ambiguity already noted in the three previous web variants.
  • lines 176–192: [enum Role { admin, user; ... }] — replaces the union of strings [TypeScript] and [type Role = 'ADMIN' | 'USER'] with an enumeration of VRAIE and [Dart], with an explicit round trip to the string JSON ([depuisChaine]/[versChaine])—which is safer (it is impossible to generate an invalid [Role]), at the cost of a conversion that a string union does not need to perform.
